title: Israel election: Anti-Netanyahu bloc ahead, but no majority
summary: While Netanyahu's party is projected to be the biggest in parliament, the anti-Netanyahu coalition looks set to have more seats. But no bloc has a clear majority.
byline: Mark Hallam, Felix Tamsut, Roshni Majumdar, Matt Ford

image.caption: Supporters of the main opposition party Yashar celebrate after exit polls suggested they were on course to win 21 seatsImage: Jack Guez/AFP

blocks.text: Ra'am party becomes political power broker

blocks.caption: Tuesday was a success for Abbas's Ra'am partyImage: Rami Shlush/REUTERS

blocks.text: The success of Ra'am, which exit polls predict will take seven seats, means no Israeli government can be established without the religious Muslim party playing some part.

The party already made headlines after appointing Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish former high-ranking police chief, as the number two candidate to leader Mansour Abbas. The raging criminality and violence across the Arab and Palestinian community, as well as the war in Gaza, both could have played a role in Ra'am's result.

Both the Likud-led coalition and large parts of the Israeli opposition may have ruled out a coalition with Ra'am, but the current results may leave them little choice but to seek some form of cooperation with the party.
As one Israeli pollster put it, "Tonight, Israelis were reminded that their population also includes Arabs and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship."
